cor-closed-bounded-compact.title: Closed and Bounded Is Compact, in Every Norm
cor-closed-bounded-compact.title_html: Closed and Bounded Is Compact, in Every Norm
cor-closed-bounded-compact.html: Let V be finite-dimensional over R or C. Call a subset K⊆V bounded for a norm if K⊆{v:‖v‖≤R} for some real R, and closed for that norm if whenever ‖uk−u‖→0 with every uk∈K, also u∈K. Then a subset that is closed and bounded for one norm is closed and bounded for every norm, and is compact: every sequence in it has a subsequence converging to a point of it. In particular, when V≠{0}, the unit sphere {v:‖v‖=1} of any norm is non-empty and compact, and a continuous real-valued function on it attains a maximum and a minimum.

cor-convergence-norm-independent.title: Convergence and Boundedness Do Not Depend on the Norm
cor-convergence-norm-independent.title_html: Convergence and Boundedness Do Not Depend on the Norm
cor-convergence-norm-independent.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional over R or C, let ‖⋅‖a and ‖⋅‖b be norms on V, and let (uk) be a sequence in V with u∈V. Then:

  1. ‖uk−u‖a→0 if and only if ‖uk−u‖b→0;
  2. (uk) is bounded for ‖⋅‖a if and only if it is bounded for ‖⋅‖b;
  3. (uk) is Cauchy for ‖⋅‖a if and only if it is Cauchy for ‖⋅‖b.

cor-derivative-of-det-at-identity.title: The Determinant’s Derivative at the Identity Is the Trace
cor-derivative-of-det-at-identity.title_html: The Determinant’s Derivative at the Identity Is the Trace
cor-derivative-of-det-at-identity.html: For every B∈Mn(C), ddt|t=0det(I+tB)=trB.

cor-diagonalizable-dense-again.title: Diagonalizable Matrices Are Dense
cor-diagonalizable-dense-again.html: Let ‖⋅‖ be any norm on Mn(C). For every A∈Mn(C) and every ε>0 there is a diagonalizable A′∈Mn(C) with ‖A−A′‖<ε. Equivalently, every complex square matrix is the limit of a sequence of diagonalizable matrices, in every norm.

cor-eigenvalues-continuous.title: Eigenvalues Depend Continuously on the Matrix
cor-eigenvalues-continuous.title_html: Eigenvalues Depend Continuously on the Matrix
cor-eigenvalues-continuous.html: Let A∈Mn(C) with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn listed with algebraic multiplicity, let ‖⋅‖ be any norm on Mn(C), and let ε>0. Then there is δ>0 such that every B∈Mn(C) with ‖B−A‖<δ has eigenvalues μ1,…,μn, listed with algebraic multiplicity, which can be numbered so that |μi−λi|<ε for every i.

cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-converg.title: Entrywise Convergence Is Convergence in Every Norm
cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-converg.title_html: Entrywise Convergence Is Convergence in Every Norm
cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-converg.html: Let M1,M2,… and M lie in Mp×q(C), and let ‖⋅‖ be any norm on Mp×q(C). Then Mk→M entrywise in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence if and only if ‖Mk−M‖→0. Likewise (Mk) is bounded in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence if and only if (‖Mk‖) is a bounded sequence of real numbers.

cor-identity-by-density.title: Proving an Identity by Density
cor-identity-by-density.html: Let Φ:Mn(C)→Mr×s(C) be a map each of whose output entries is a polynomial in the entries of the input. If Φ(A)=0 for every diagonalizable A∈Mn(C), then Φ(A)=0 for every A∈Mn(C).

cor-invertible-matrices-open.title: Invertibility Is an Open Condition, and Inversion Is Continuous
cor-invertible-matrices-open.title_html: Invertibility Is an Open Condition, and Inversion Is Continuous
cor-invertible-matrices-open.html:
Let B∈Mn(C) be invertible and let E∈Mn(C) satisfy ‖E‖<1‖B−1‖. Write r=‖B−1‖‖E‖<1. Then:

  1. B+E is invertible, and ‖(B+E)−1‖≤‖B−1‖1−r;
  2. ‖(B+E)−1−B−1‖≤‖B−1‖2‖E‖1−r.

Consequently GLn(C) is an open subset of Mn(C): around every invertible B the ball of radius 1/‖B−1‖ consists of invertible matrices. And inversion is continuous on it: if Bm→B with B invertible, then Bm is invertible for all large m and Bm−1→B−1.

cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one.title: Powers Tending to Zero, with a Rate
cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one.title_html: Powers Tending to Zero, with a Rate
cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and let ‖⋅‖ be any matrix norm on Mn(C).

  1. Ak→0 if and only if ρ(A)<1, and this holds if and only if ‖Ak‖→0.
  2. If ρ(A)<1, then for every q with ρ(A)<q<1 there is a constant C≥1, depending on A, on q and on the norm, such that ‖Ak‖≤Cqk for every k≥0.

cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound.title: Cheap Bounds on the Spectrum
cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound.html:
Let A∈Mn(C). Then every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies

|λ|≤ρ(A)≤min{‖A‖1, ‖A‖∞, ‖A‖F},

that is, ρ(A) is at most the largest absolute column sum, at most the largest absolute row sum, and at most ‖A‖F.

def-condition-number.title: Condition Number
def-condition-number.html: Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Cn, and write ‖⋅‖ also for the operator norm it induces on Mn(C). For A∈Mn(C), the condition number of A with respect to that norm is κ(A):={‖A‖‖A−1‖if A is invertible,∞if A is singular. We write κ1,κ2,κ∞ for the condition numbers with respect to ‖⋅‖1, ‖⋅‖2, ‖⋅‖∞; κ2 is also called the spectral condition number. For a rectangular A∈Mm×n(C) with m≥n and rankA=n, we define κ2(A):=σ1(A)σn(A), the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value (@def-singular-values).

def-equivalent-norms.title: Equivalent Norms
def-equivalent-norms.html: Let V be a vector space over F=R or C, and let ‖⋅‖a and ‖⋅‖b be norms on V. They are equivalent if there exist real constants c,C>0, not depending on the vector, such that c‖v‖b ≤ ‖v‖a ≤ C‖v‖bfor every v∈V.

def-matrix-norm.title: Matrix Norm
def-matrix-norm.html:
Let n≥1. A matrix norm on Mn(F) is a function ‖⋅‖:Mn(F)→R which is a norm on Mn(F) as a vector space (@def-norm) and which is in addition submultiplicative: for all A,B∈Mn(F),

‖AB‖≤‖A‖‖B‖.

def-matrix-valued-derivative.title: Derivative of a Matrix-Valued Function
def-matrix-valued-derivative.html: Let I⊆R be an open interval and A:I→Mm×n(C), written A(t)=(aij(t)). Call A differentiable at t0∈I if every entry function aij:I→C is differentiable at t0, and then set A′(t0):=(aij′(t0))∈Mm×n(C).

def-norm.title: Norm
def-norm.html:
Let F be R or C and let V be a vector space over F. A norm on V is a function ‖⋅‖:V→R such that for all u,v∈V and all c∈F:

  1. ‖v‖≥0, and ‖v‖=0 only for v=0 (positive definiteness);
  2. ‖cv‖=|c|‖v‖ (absolute homogeneity);
  3. ‖u+v‖≤‖u‖+‖v‖ (the triangle inequality).

A vector space carrying a norm is a normed space. A vector with ‖v‖=1 is a unit vector, and replacing a non-zero v by v/‖v‖ is normalizing it.

def-operator-norm.title: Operator Norm
def-operator-norm.html:
Let n,m≥1 and let a norm ‖⋅‖ be given on Fn and on Fm; we write both with the same symbol, the argument saying which is meant. The operator norm of A∈Mm×n(F) induced by those norms is

‖A‖:=max{‖Ax‖:x∈Fn, ‖x‖=1},

which exists by @lem-operator-norm-attained. When the vector norm is ‖⋅‖p on both sides we write ‖A‖p, and ‖A‖2 is also called the spectral norm.

def-spectral-radius.title: Spectral Radius
def-spectral-radius.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) with n≥1. The spectral radius of A is

ρ(A):=max{|λ|:λ∈spec(A)}.

For an operator T on a non-zero finite-dimensional complex vector space, ρ(T) is defined by the same formula with spec(T) in place of spec(A).

def-unit-ball.title: Closed Unit Ball
def-unit-ball.html: Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on V. Its closed unit ball is B‖⋅‖={v∈V:‖v‖≤1}. In Fn we write B1, B2 and B∞ for the balls of @exm-p-norms.

exm-cayley-hamilton-by-density.html: Prove that pA(A)=0 for every A∈Mn(C), using density rather than the adjugate identity of @thm-adjugate-identity.

exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative.title: The entrywise maximum is not submultiplicative
exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative.title_html: The entrywise maximum is not submultiplicative
exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative.html: For A∈Mn(F) put N(A)=maxi,j|aij|. Show that N is a norm on Mn(F) but not a matrix norm for n≥2.

exm-exponential-bound-sharp-and-not.title_html: Where the bound is exact, and where it is useless

exm-frobenius-distance-to-a-limit.title: Watching one sequence converge
exm-frobenius-distance-to-a-limit.html: In M2(R) let Mk=(1k201−1k),k≥1. Entry by entry, 1k→0, 2→2, 0→0 and 1−1k→1, so Mk→M=(0201) in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence. The corollary says this is convergence in every norm, and here one can see it directly: Mk−M=diag(1k,−1k), so ‖Mk−M‖F=1k2+1k2=2k⟶0, and ‖Mk−M‖∞, the largest absolute row sum, is 1k. Different norms, different constants, the same verdict — which is the content of the corollary.

exm-frobenius-is-a-matrix-norm.title: The Frobenius norm is submultiplicative
exm-frobenius-is-a-matrix-norm.html: Show that ‖AB‖F≤‖A‖F‖B‖F for all A,B∈Mn(F), so that ‖⋅‖F is a matrix norm.

exm-gelfand-triangular.title: Watching the limit converge
exm-gelfand-triangular.html: Let A=(1/21001/3). Compute ‖Ak‖∞ exactly and confirm Gelfand’s formula.

exm-ill-conditioned-system.title_html: A system where the bound is attained

exm-induced-and-weighted-norms.title: Inner products, weights, and a function space
exm-induced-and-weighted-norms.title_html: Inner products, weights, and a function space
exm-induced-and-weighted-norms.html:
Three further families.

  1. Every inner product gives a norm. If V is an inner product space, then ‖v‖=⟨v,v⟩ satisfies (N1) and (N2) by @thm-norm-properties (a), (b) and (N3) by @cor-triangle-inequality. In particular the Frobenius norm ‖A‖F on Mm×n(F) and the norm (∫01|f|2)1/2 on C[0,1] are norms.
  2. Weighted norms. Fix real weights w1,…,wn>0 and put ‖x‖w=maxiwi|xi|. All three clauses go through exactly as for ‖⋅‖∞, the weights riding along untouched; positivity of every wi is what (N1) needs.
  3. The sup norm. On C[0,1], the real continuous functions on [0,1], put ‖f‖∞=maxt∈[0,1]|f(t)|.

  2. Compute (A−1)′(0) by @thm-derivative-of-inverse, and check it against a direct expansion.

exm-jordan-block-perturbation.title_html: A Jordan block’s eigenvalues move like ε1/k

exm-neumann-bound-two-by-two.title: The bound and the truth
exm-neumann-bound-two-by-two.html: Let A=(01/21/30). Using the ∞-norm, check the hypothesis, compute (I−A)−1 exactly, and compare it with the bound of @thm-neumann-series (b). Then compare S3 with the true inverse and with the tail bound of (c).

exm-norm-equivalence-constants.title: The three p-norms, with best constants
exm-norm-equivalence-constants.title_html: The three p-norms, with best constants
exm-norm-equivalence-constants.html: On Fn, @prp-p-norm-inequalities gives ‖x‖∞≤‖x‖2≤n‖x‖∞,‖x‖∞≤‖x‖1≤n‖x‖∞,1n‖x‖1≤‖x‖2≤‖x‖1, so the three are pairwise equivalent. The middle line’s upper constant comes from ‖x‖1≤n‖x‖2≤n⋅n‖x‖∞. Every constant shown is attained, so none of them can be improved. On the first two lines the lower constant is attained at e1 and the upper one at 1. The third line runs the other way: at 1 the lower inequality reads 1n⋅n=n≤n, and at e1 the upper one reads 1≤1.

exm-norm-non-example.title: Three near misses
exm-norm-non-example.html:
Change one feature of an example above and watch a single clause break.

  1. Drop the square root. On Fn put N(x)=|x1|2+⋯+|xn|2. Then (N1) still holds. But N(cx)=|c|2N(x), so (N2) fails as soon as |c|≠0,1: for x=e1 and c=2 it gives N(2e1)=4≠2=|2|N(e1). The square root in ‖⋅‖2 is there for exactly this reason.
  2. Forget a coordinate. On F2 put N(x)=|x1|. Then (N2) and (N3) both hold, inherited from |⋅| on F. What fails is the word only in (N1): N(e2)=0 while e2≠0. A function satisfying (N1) with “only” deleted, together with (N2) and (N3), is called a seminorm; it measures a quotient of V rather than V.
  3. Bend the exponent the other way. On R2 put N(x)=(|x1|1/2+|x2|1/2)2. Then (N1) holds, and (N2) holds because |c|1/2 factors out of the inner sum and is squared back to |c|. Only (N3) fails: N(e1)=N(e2)=1 but N(e1+e2)=(1+1)2=4>2.

exm-normal-equations-squaring.title: Squaring, on a 3 \times 2 example
exm-normal-equations-squaring.title_html: Squaring, on a 3×2 example
exm-normal-equations-squaring.html: Let A=(110.1000.1). Compute κ2(A) and κ2(A⊤A).

exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimens.title: Two inequivalent norms on a space of polynomials
exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimens.title_html: Two inequivalent norms on a space of polynomials
exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimens.html: Let V=R[x], the real polynomials — equivalently, the sequences of real coefficients with only finitely many non-zero terms. For p=a0+a1x+⋯+adxd put ‖p‖1=|a0|+⋯+|ad|,‖p‖∞=maxi|ai|. Both are norms, by the same coordinatewise checks as in @exm-p-norms; the only difference is that the number of coordinates is unbounded. One inequality survives: ‖p‖∞≤‖p‖1 always. The other fails completely. Put pk=1+x+x2+⋯+xk−1. Then ‖pk‖1=k while ‖pk‖∞=1, so a constant C with ‖p‖1≤C‖p‖∞ for all p would have to satisfy C≥k for every k. No such C exists, and the two norms are not equivalent.

exm-oblique-projection-norm.title: The oblique projection, finally measured
exm-oblique-projection-norm.html: Chapter 12 §12 studied a projection P of F2 onto a line, with matrix (1x00) in a suitable orthonormal basis, and found that the largest value of ‖Pv‖ over unit v is 1+|x|2, which over R is 1/sin⁡θ for the angle θ between image and kernel. Confirm this with @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c) for x=−1, the matrix P′=(1−100) of @exm-oblique-projection-2x2.

exm-openness-with-numbers.title: How far an invertible matrix can be pushed
exm-openness-with-numbers.title_html: How far an invertible matrix can be pushed
exm-openness-with-numbers.html: Take B=(2102) and work with ‖⋅‖∞. Then B−1=(12−14012), whose largest absolute row sum is 12+14=34, so ‖B−1‖∞=34. @cor-invertible-matrices-open therefore keeps B+E invertible for every E with ‖E‖∞<1‖B−1‖∞=43. For a perturbation of size ‖E‖∞≤12 we get r=34⋅12=38, and part (a) bounds ‖(B+E)−1‖∞ ≤ 3/41−3/8 = 65. The bound is honest rather than tight: pushing every entry of E to ±14 gives at worst ‖(B+E)−1‖∞=1211≈1.09, against the promised 1.2. What the corollary buys is not the sharpest constant but a radius inside which no invertibility check is needed at all.

exm-two-norms-agree-on-a-basis.title_html: Agreeing on a basis is not enough

exr-condition-numbers-c1.title_html: C1: Changing the norm changes κ, but not much

exr-condition-numbers-c2.title_html: C2: The condition number is the reciprocal distance to singularity

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b1.title_html: B1: Two perturbations of the same size
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b1.html: Let ε=10−8. Compute the eigenvalues of B=(01ε0)andC=(ε100), each of which differs from J2(0) by a matrix of 2-norm ε. Hence explain why the constant in @cor-eigenvalues-continuous cannot depend on ‖B−A‖ alone.

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b2.title: B2: A diagonalizable neighbor, explicitly
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b2.html:
Let A=(2102) and let ε>0.

  1. Show that A is not diagonalizable.
  2. Exhibit a diagonalizable A′ with ‖A−A′‖2<ε, and say which theorem certifies that your A′ is diagonalizable.
  3. What are the eigenvalues of your A′, and how far have they moved?

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b3.title: B3: The determinant and the trace, by density
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b3.title_html: B3: The determinant and the trace, by density
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-b3.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C). Use @cor-identity-by-density to prove that tr(AB)=tr(BA) — after first checking that the map in question satisfies the hypothesis of that corollary — and then explain why this is a bad way to prove it.

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c1.title: C1: How close to singular a nearby eigenvalue forces you to be
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c1.title_html: C1: How close to singular a nearby eigenvalue forces you to be
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), let ‖⋅‖ be an operator norm on Mn(C) (@def-operator-norm) and let E∈Mn(C) with E≠0.

  1. Suppose μ is an eigenvalue of A+E and μ∉spec(A). Prove that ‖(A−μI)−1‖≥1‖E‖.
  2. Deduce that if ‖(A−zI)−1‖≤M for every z with |z−λ|=r, then no eigenvalue of A+E lies on that circle as soon as ‖E‖<1/M.

Hint: for (a), factor A+E−μI and use @thm-neumann-series.

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c2.title: C2: Density of the invertible matrices, and \A\B versus \B\A
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c2.title_html: C2: Density of the invertible matrices, and AB versus BA
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c2.html:
1. Prove that for every A∈Mn(C) and every ε>0 there is an invertible A′ with ‖A−A′‖<ε, in any norm. Hint: consider A−tI.
  2. Prove a version of @cor-identity-by-density with “invertible” in place of “diagonalizable”.
  3. Hence give a second proof that pAB=pBA for all A,B∈Mn(C), a statement first proved in @thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues (b).

exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c3.title: C3: Distinct eigenvalues is an open condition
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c3.title_html: C3: Distinct eigenvalues is an open condition
exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) have n distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, and let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Mn(C).

  1. Prove that there is δ>0 such that every B with ‖B−A‖<δ also has n distinct eigenvalues, and is therefore diagonalizable.
  2. Deduce that the set of matrices in Mn(C) with a repeated eigenvalue contains no ball, that is, that its complement is dense.
  3. Is the set of diagonalizable matrices open? Justify your answer.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-a1.title: A1
exr-equivalence-of-norms-a1.html:
1. State @def-equivalent-norms, and explain why the phrase “not depending on the vector” cannot be dropped.
  2. State @thm-norm-equivalence, including its hypothesis on V.
  3. Which two of the four imported analysis facts does the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence use, and at which step is each used?
  4. True or false: if two norms on Rn are equivalent, then some sequence converges in one and not the other. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: equivalent norms give the same value to every vector. Justify your answer.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-b1.title: B1: Best constants for a weighted norm
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b1.title_html: B1: Best constants for a weighted norm
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b1.html: On R2 let N(x)=(x12+4x22)1/2. Find the best constants c,C>0 with c‖x‖∞≤N(x)≤C‖x‖∞(x∈R2), and give a vector attaining each. Hence deduce that N and ‖⋅‖∞ are equivalent.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-b2.title: B2: Reading a convergence off the entries
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b2.title_html: B2: Reading a convergence off the entries
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b2.html: In M2(R) let Mk=(1+1k(−1)kk212k3−5k). Determine limkMk in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence, and compute ‖Mk−M‖F explicitly. Hence confirm @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence for this sequence and the Frobenius norm.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-b3.title: B3: An equivalence with the constants written down
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b3.title_html: B3: An equivalence with the constants written down
exr-equivalence-of-norms-b3.html:
Let V=R[x]≤2 with basis B=(1,x,x2). For p∈V let ‖p‖B be the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector, and let N(p)=|p(0)|+|p(1)|+|p(−1)|.

  1. Prove that N is a norm on V.
  2. Find an explicit M with N(p)≤M‖p‖B, following Step 1 of the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence.
  3. Explain, without computing it, why a constant m>0 with N(p)≥m‖p‖B exists.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-c1.title: C1: Every linear map out of a finite-dimensional space is continuous
exr-equivalence-of-norms-c1.title_html: C1: Every linear map out of a finite-dimensional space is continuous
exr-equivalence-of-norms-c1.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional over F with norm ‖⋅‖V, let W be a normed space over F with norm ‖⋅‖W, and let T:V→W be linear. Fix a basis B=(v1,…,vn) of V and write ‖⋅‖1 for the 1-norm of the coordinate vector in the basis B.

  1. Prove that ‖Tv‖W≤K‖v‖1 for every v∈V, where K=maxi‖Tvi‖W.
  2. Hence prove that there is a constant L with ‖Tu−Tv‖W≤L‖u−v‖V for all u,v∈V.
  3. Explain why (b) may fail when V is infinite-dimensional, using @exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimension.

exr-equivalence-of-norms-c2.title: C2: No dimension-free constants
exr-equivalence-of-norms-c2.html:
For each n≥1 let cn,Cn>0 be the best constants with cn‖x‖∞≤‖x‖1≤Cn‖x‖∞(x∈Fn).

  1. Determine cn and Cn, with a vector attaining each.
  2. Deduce that there is no pair of constants c,C>0 working simultaneously for every n.
  3. A statement about Rn says “the error e satisfies ‖e‖∞≤10−6”. What is the strongest bound on ‖e‖1 that follows, and for which n does it stop being informative if the entries of e are themselves of size about 10−6?

exr-equivalence-of-norms-c3.title: C3: A finite-dimensional subspace is closed
exr-equivalence-of-norms-c3.title_html: C3: A finite-dimensional subspace is closed
exr-equivalence-of-norms-c3.html:
Let W be a normed space over F with norm ‖⋅‖, and let U⊆W be a finite-dimensional subspace. Let (uk) be a sequence in U with ‖uk−w‖→0 for some w∈W.

  1. Prove that (uk) is bounded in U for the restricted norm.
  2. Using @cor-closed-bounded-compact, produce a subsequence (ukj) converging to some u∈U.
  3. Deduce that w=u, so that U contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its own elements. Hint: the triangle inequality, through ukj.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-a1.title: A1
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-a1.html:
1. Define a matrix norm on Mn(F), and define the operator norm induced by a vector norm.
  2. State the three formulas of @thm-operator-norm-formulas.
  3. Which analysis facts make @def-operator-norm legitimate, and where is each used?
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: every matrix norm on Mn(R) is the operator norm induced by some norm on Rn.
  5. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: for every A∈Mn(F) and every operator norm, ‖A2‖=‖A‖2.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b1.title: B1: Four numbers for one matrix
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b1.title_html: B1: Four numbers for one matrix
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b1.html: Let A=(2−122)∈M2(R). Compute ‖A‖1, ‖A‖∞, ‖A‖F and ‖A‖2, and verify that ‖A‖2≤‖A‖F.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b2.title: B2: A rank-one matrix
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b2.html:
Let u∈Fm and v∈Fn be non-zero and put A=uv∗.

  1. Prove that ‖A‖2=‖u‖2‖v‖2.
  2. Verify the formula for u=(1,2) and v=(2,−1) in R2 by computing σ1(A) directly.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b3.title: B3: The star trick
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-b3.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). Prove that ‖A∗A‖2=‖A‖22. Hint: the eigenvalues of A∗A.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c1.title: C1: The spectral norm between the other two
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c1.title_html: C1: The spectral norm between the other two
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Prove that ‖A‖2≤‖A‖1‖A‖∞.
  2. Check the inequality on the matrix of @exm-three-norms-of-a-matrix, and say how far it is from equality.

Hint for (a): apply @thm-cauchy-schwarz to the splitting |aij|=|aij|1/2⋅|aij|1/2|xj| inside one row.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c2.title: C2: Repairing the entrywise maximum
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c2.html:
For A∈Mn(F) let N(A)=maxi,j|aij|, as in @exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative.

  1. Prove that N(AB)≤nN(A)N(B), and deduce that A↦nN(A) is a matrix norm.
  2. Deduce that nN(⋅) is not an operator norm for any n≥2.
  3. Explain why (a) and (b) together show that submultiplicativity and ‖I‖=1 are independent requirements.

exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c3.title: C3: When is a bound an equality?
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c3.title_html: C3: When is a bound an equality?
exr-matrix-and-operator-norms-c3.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) be non-zero.

  1. Prove that ‖A‖2=‖A‖F if and only if rankA=1.
  2. Give an example with m=n=2 where ‖A‖F=2‖A‖2, the worst case allowed by @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius.
  3. Is there a non-zero A with ‖A‖F<‖A‖2? Justify your answer.

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-a1.title: A1
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-a1.html:
1. State the three bounds of @thm-exponential-norm-bound, and say which property of the norm each one needs.
  2. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if ‖A‖2 is large then ‖eA‖2 is large.
  3. State @thm-exponential-decay, and say what the constant C is paying for.
  4. State Jacobi’s formula (@thm-derivative-of-det), and name the fact from calculus its proof quotes.
  5. Write down the derivative of t↦A(t)−1 and explain in one sentence why it is not −A−2A′.

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b1.title: B1: Bound against truth
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b1.html:
For each matrix, compute ‖eA‖∞ exactly and compare with e‖A‖∞.

  1. A=(0300).
  2. A=diag(1,−4).

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b2.title: B2: A rate for a stable matrix
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b2.title_html: B2: A rate for a stable matrix
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b2.html:
Let A=(−240−2).

  1. Compute μ and etA, and give ‖etA‖∞ for t≥0.
  2. Find the largest value of ‖etA‖∞ on t≥0.
  3. Find the smallest C that works in @thm-exponential-decay for ν=−1.

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b3.title: B3: Two derivatives
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-b3.html:
Let A(t)=(cos⁡t−sin⁡tsin⁡tcos⁡t).

  1. Compute ddtdetA(t) by @thm-derivative-of-det and check it against the exact value of detA(t).
  2. Compute (A−1)′(t) by @thm-derivative-of-inverse and check it by differentiating A(t)−1 directly.

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c1.title: C1: The determinant of the exponential, again
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c1.title_html: C1: The determinant of the exponential, again
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and put φ(t)=detetA.

  1. Prove that φ is differentiable with φ′(t)=(trA)φ(t).
  2. Hence deduce deteA=etrA, recovering @thm-exponential-properties (e).

Hint for (b): consider ψ(t)=e−ttrAφ(t).

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c2.title: C2: Comparing two exponentials
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(C) with AB=BA.

  1. Prove that ‖eA−eB‖≤e‖B‖(e‖A−B‖−1).
  2. Deduce that M↦eM is continuous at every M that commutes with a neighborhood of itself, and identify those M: they are exactly the scalar matrices cI.
  3. Say exactly where the commuting hypothesis is used, and why the argument cannot simply be dropped.

exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c3.title: C3: A quantity that measures the decay
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c3.title_html: C3: A quantity that measures the decay
exr-matrix-exponential-and-calculus-c3.html:
Let A,X,Q∈Mn(C) with X and Q positive definite (@def-positive-semidefinite) and A∗X+XA=−Q. Let x:R→Cn be differentiable with x′=Ax, and put V(t)=x(t)∗Xx(t).

  1. Prove that V is real-valued and differentiable, with V′(t)=x(t)∗(A∗X+XA)x(t).
  2. Deduce that if x(0)≠0, then V is strictly decreasing.
  3. Explain how this relates to the Lyapunov equation of @def-lyapunov-equation, whose unknown sits between A and A∗ the other way round.

Hint for (a): x∗ is a 1×n matrix-valued function, and f―′=f′― for a differentiable f:R→C.

exr-neumann-series-a1.title: A1
exr-neumann-series-a1.html:
1. State @thm-neumann-series in full, including which kind of norm it assumes.
  2. Chapter 9 §10 already proved that ∑kAk converges to (I−A)−1 when ρ(A)<1. Say precisely what this section adds, and what it gives up.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if I−A is invertible then ‖A‖<1.
  4. Where in the proof of @thm-neumann-series is ‖I‖=1 used?
  5. State what @cor-invertible-matrices-open says about the distance from an invertible matrix to the singular matrices.

exr-neumann-series-b1.title: B1: Check, sum, compare
exr-neumann-series-b1.html:
Let A=(1/41/401/2).

  1. Verify the hypothesis of @thm-neumann-series for ‖⋅‖∞.
  2. Compute (I−A)−1 exactly and compare ‖(I−A)−1‖∞ with the bound of (b) and with the lower bound of (d).

exr-neumann-series-b2.title: B2: A perturbed right-hand side
exr-neumann-series-b2.html: Let A=(3112), b=(4,3) and f=(1/10,0), with E=0. Solve both systems, compute the relative error in the ∞-norm, and compare with @thm-perturbed-inverse-bound.

exr-neumann-series-b3.title: B3: Staying invertible
exr-neumann-series-b3.html: Let B=(2001/2). Using ‖⋅‖∞, find a radius δ>0 such that every E with ‖E‖∞<δ leaves B+E invertible, and bound ‖(B+E)−1‖∞ for ‖E‖∞≤14. Is your δ the largest possible?

exr-neumann-series-c1.title: C1: The inverse to first order
exr-neumann-series-c1.title_html: C1: The inverse to first order
exr-neumann-series-c1.html:
Let ‖A‖<1.

  1. Prove that ‖(I−A)−1−I−A‖≤‖A‖21−‖A‖.
  2. Deduce that for a fixed M∈Mn(C) and small real t, (I−tM)−1=I+tM+R(t),‖R(t)‖/|t|→0 as t→0.

Hint for (a): this is @thm-neumann-series (c) with a particular K.

exr-neumann-series-c2.title: C2: Distance to the singular matrices
exr-neumann-series-c2.title_html: C2: Distance to the singular matrices
exr-neumann-series-c2.html:
Let B∈Mn(C) be invertible and let ‖⋅‖ be an induced matrix norm.

  1. Prove that every singular S∈Mn(C) satisfies ‖B−S‖≥1/‖B−1‖.
  2. For B=diag(1,ε) with 0<ε<1 and the 2-norm, exhibit a singular S attaining the bound.
  3. Hence say what ‖B−1‖2 measures.

exr-neumann-series-c3.title: C3: Without \norm{\I} = 1
exr-neumann-series-c3.title_html: C3: Without ‖I‖=1
exr-neumann-series-c3.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ be any matrix norm on Mn(C) in the sense of @def-matrix-norm, not necessarily induced, and let ‖A‖<1.

  1. Prove that I−A is invertible and that ‖(I−A)−1‖≤‖I‖+‖A‖1−‖A‖.
  2. Verify that this bound is correct for the Frobenius norm on M2(C) with A=0, where the bound of @thm-neumann-series (b) fails.
  3. Explain why the argument of (a) cannot be improved to 1/(1−‖A‖) for a general matrix norm.

exr-spectral-radius-a1.title: A1
exr-spectral-radius-a1.html:
1. Define the spectral radius, and say why the maximum in the definition exists.
  2. State @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm and @thm-gelfand.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: ρ is a matrix norm on Mn(C).
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if ρ(A)<1 then ‖A‖2<1.
  5. Chapter 9 §10 already proved that Am→0 exactly when ρ(A)<1. What does @cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one add to that?

exr-spectral-radius-b1.title: B1: Four numbers again
exr-spectral-radius-b1.html: Let A=(021/40). Compute ρ(A), ‖A‖1, ‖A‖∞ and ‖A‖2, and verify @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm in each case.

exr-spectral-radius-b2.title: B2: Gelfand exactly
exr-spectral-radius-b2.html: With A as in @exr-spectral-radius-b1, compute Ak for every k and evaluate limk‖Ak‖∞1/k directly.

exr-spectral-radius-b3.title: B3: Deciding convergence without eigenvalues
exr-spectral-radius-b3.html:
For each matrix, decide whether Am→0, using only @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound and @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero.

  1. A=14(120011201).
  2. A=(1/2302).

exr-spectral-radius-c1.title: C1: A norm that sees the decay
exr-spectral-radius-c1.title_html: C1: A norm that sees the decay
exr-spectral-radius-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. Prove that if ‖A‖<1 for some matrix norm, then Ak→0.
  2. Give a matrix with Ak→0 and ‖A‖2>1, so that the converse of (a) fails for a fixed norm.
  3. Prove that the converse of (a) nevertheless holds if the norm is allowed to depend on A.

exr-spectral-radius-c2.title: C2: Spectral radius zero
exr-spectral-radius-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. Prove that ρ(A)=0 if and only if A is nilpotent.
  2. Deduce that for a nilpotent A and any matrix norm, ‖Ak‖1/k→0, and verify this directly for A=Jn(0).
  3. Explain why (a) shows that no inequality of the form ‖A‖≤cρ(A), with c depending only on n, can hold.

exr-spectral-radius-c3.title: C3: When the infimum is attained
exr-spectral-radius-c3.title_html: C3: When the infimum is attained
exr-spectral-radius-c3.html:
Call A∈Mn(C) radius-attaining if ‖A‖=ρ(A) for some matrix norm.

  1. Prove that every normal A is radius-attaining.
  2. Prove that a non-zero nilpotent A is not.
  3. Deduce that (1101) is not radius-attaining, even though it is invertible.

Hint for (c): consider A−I.

exr-vector-norms-a1.title: A1
exr-vector-norms-a1.html:
1. State the three clauses of @def-norm, and say which one fails for N(x)=|x1| on F2.
  2. Deduce ‖0‖=0 from (N2) alone, and explain why (N1) is therefore stated with the word only.
  3. True or false: a function satisfying (N1) and (N3) but not (N2) cannot exist. Justify your answer.
  4. Name the test that decides whether a norm is induced by an inner product, and state what @exr-inner-products-c1 had already established before this section.
  5. Order ‖x‖1, ‖x‖2, ‖x‖∞ for a general x∈Fn, and give a vector for which all three are equal.

exr-vector-norms-b1.title: B1: Three measurements
exr-vector-norms-b1.html: For x=(1,−1,2,−2)∈R4, compute ‖x‖1, ‖x‖2 and ‖x‖∞, and verify all four inequalities of @prp-p-norm-inequalities. Which of them is closest to being an equality?

exr-vector-norms-b2.title: B2: Determine which are norms
exr-vector-norms-b2.html:
Determine which of the following define norms on R2. For those that do, verify all three clauses of @def-norm; for those that do not, name the exact clause that fails and give a witness. Justify your answer.

  1. N(x)=|x1|+2|x2|.
  2. N(x)=|x1−x2|.
  3. N(x)=max(|x1|,|x2|)−14min(|x1|,|x2|).
  4. N(x)=|x1|+|x2|−12min(|x1|,|x2|).

exr-vector-norms-b3.title: B3: Which of these come from an inner product?
exr-vector-norms-b3.title_html: B3: Which of these come from an inner product?
exr-vector-norms-b3.html:
For each norm, determine whether it is induced by an inner product. Justify your answer, using @thm-parallelogram-characterization in each case.

  1. ‖x‖=(x12+x1x2+x22)1/2 on R2.
  2. ‖A‖F on M2(R).
  3. N(A)=maxi,j|aij| on M2(R).

exr-vector-norms-c1.title: C1: Sharpness of the comparison constants
exr-vector-norms-c1.title_html: C1: Sharpness of the comparison constants
exr-vector-norms-c1.html:
1. Prove that ‖x‖1=n‖x‖2 holds if and only if all the numbers |x1|,…,|xn| are equal. Hint: the equality case of @thm-cauchy-schwarz.
  2. Hence deduce that no constant C independent of n satisfies ‖x‖1≤C‖x‖2 for all n and all x∈Rn.

exr-vector-norms-c2.title: C2: A real norm that is not a complex norm
exr-vector-norms-c2.title_html: C2: A real norm that is not a complex norm
exr-vector-norms-c2.html:
Regard C as a one-dimensional complex vector space, and also as R2 by z=a+bi↔(a,b). Define N(z)=2|a|+|b|.

  1. Prove that N is a norm on R2.
  2. Prove that N is not a norm on C as a complex vector space, and name the exact clause that fails.
  3. Prove that if ‖⋅‖ is any norm on a complex vector space V, then it is also a norm on V regarded as a real vector space. Explain why (b) does not contradict this.

exr-vector-norms-c3.title: C3: The ball determines the norm
exr-vector-norms-c3.title_html: C3: The ball determines the norm
exr-vector-norms-c3.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ and N be two norms on a vector space V with the same closed unit ball, in the sense of @def-unit-ball: {v:‖v‖≤1}={v:N(v)≤1}.

  1. Prove that for every v∈V and every real t>0, we have ‖v‖≤t if and only if v/t lies in the closed unit ball of ‖⋅‖.
  2. Hence prove that ‖v‖=N(v) for every v∈V.
  3. Give two different norms on R2 whose closed unit balls have the same area, and say why (b) does not apply to them.

lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous.title: Polynomial Maps of the Entries Are Continuous
lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous.title_html: Polynomial Maps of the Entries Are Continuous
lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous.html: Let Φ:Mp×q(C)→Mr×s(C) be a map each of whose output entries is given by a fixed polynomial, with complex coefficients, in the pq entries of the input. Fix any norm on the source and any norm on the target. Then Φ is continuous: whenever ‖Ak−A‖→0 we have ‖Φ(Ak)−Φ(A)‖→0, and equivalently, for every A and every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that ‖B−A‖<δ forces ‖Φ(B)−Φ(A)‖<ε. The same holds for a map into C.

lem-inverse-norm-min.title: The Inverse Measures the Smallest Stretch
lem-inverse-norm-min.title_html: The Inverse Measures the Smallest Stretch
lem-inverse-norm-min.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible and let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Cn. Then ‖A−1‖=1min{‖Ax‖:‖x‖=1},κ(A)=max{‖Ax‖:‖x‖=1}min{‖Ax‖:‖x‖=1}.

lem-matrix-product-rule.title: Product Rule for Matrices
lem-matrix-product-rule.html: Let A:I→Mm×n(C) and B:I→Mn×p(C) be differentiable at t0. Then so is t↦A(t)B(t), with (AB)′(t0)=A′(t0)B(t0)+A(t0)B′(t0).

lem-operator-norm-attained.title: The Largest Stretch Is Attained
lem-operator-norm-attained.html: Let n,m≥1, let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Fn and also a norm on Fm, and let A∈Mm×n(F). Then the function x↦‖Ax‖ attains a maximum on the unit sphere S={x∈Fn:‖x‖=1}.

lem-reverse-triangle-norm.title: Reverse Triangle Inequality
lem-reverse-triangle-norm.html: Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on V. Then for all u,v∈V, |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖.

lem-spectral-radius-of-exponential.title: The Spectrum of the Exponential
lem-spectral-radius-of-exponential.html: Let A∈Mn(C). Then spec(eA)={eλ:λ∈spec(A)}, and ρ(eA)=eμ,μ=max{Reλ:λ∈spec(A)}.

prp-condition-number-properties.title: Properties of the Condition Number
prp-condition-number-properties.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(C) be invertible and let c∈C∖{0}. With respect to any operator norm:

  1. κ(A)≥1;
  2. κ(cA)=κ(A);
  3. κ(AB)≤κ(A)κ(B);
  4. κ2(A)=σ1(A)/σn(A), and κ2(UAV)=κ2(A) for all unitary U,V.

prp-equivalence-of-norms-relation.title: Equivalence of Norms Is an Equivalence Relation
prp-equivalence-of-norms-relation.title_html: Equivalence of Norms Is an Equivalence Relation
prp-equivalence-of-norms-relation.html: On a fixed vector space V over F, the relation of @def-equivalent-norms is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

prp-no-continuous-root-selection.title: There Is No Continuous Choice of a Single Eigenvalue
prp-no-continuous-root-selection.title_html: There Is No Continuous Choice of a Single Eigenvalue
prp-no-continuous-root-selection.html: For t∈C put A(t)=(01t0), so that pA(t)(x)=x2−t and the eigenvalues of A(t) are the two square roots of t. Then there is no continuous function λ:D→C on the closed unit disc D={t∈C:|t|≤1} such that λ(t) is an eigenvalue of A(t) for every t∈D. Consequently there is no continuous Λ:M2(C)→C with Λ(B)∈spec(B) for every B.

prp-p-norm-inequalities.title: Comparing the Three Norms
prp-p-norm-inequalities.html: For every x∈Fn, ‖x‖∞≤‖x‖2≤‖x‖1 and ‖x‖1≤n‖x‖2,‖x‖2≤n‖x‖∞. Each of the four inequalities is attained: the first two by x=e1, the last two by x=1.

prp-spectral-vs-frobenius.title: Frobenius Against Spectral
prp-spectral-vs-frobenius.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) be non-zero, of rank r. Then

‖A‖2≤‖A‖F≤r‖A‖2,

and the left inequality is an equality if and only if r=1.

thm-derivative-of-det.title: Jacobi’s Formula
thm-derivative-of-det.html: Let A:I→Mn(C) be differentiable at t0∈I. Then t↦detA(t) is differentiable at t0, with ddt|t0detA(t)=tr(adjA(t0)A′(t0)). If moreover A(t0) is invertible, this equals detA(t0)tr(A(t0)−1A′(t0)).

thm-derivative-of-inverse.title: Derivative of the Inverse
thm-derivative-of-inverse.html: Let A:I→Mn(C) be differentiable at t0∈I, with A(t0) invertible. Then A(t) is invertible for all t in some open interval around t0, the function t↦A(t)−1 is differentiable at t0, and (A−1)′(t0)=−A(t0)−1A′(t0)A(t0)−1.

thm-exponential-decay.title: Exponential Decay of a Stable System
thm-exponential-decay.title_html: Exponential Decay of a Stable System
thm-exponential-decay.html: Let A∈Mn(C), let μ=max{Reλ:λ∈spec(A)}, and let ν>μ be real. Then there is a constant C≥1, depending on A, on ν and on the norm, with ‖etA‖≤Ceνtfor every t≥0. In particular, if A is stable then ν may be taken negative, and every solution of x′=Ax satisfies ‖x(t)‖≤Ceνt‖x(0)‖→t→∞0.

thm-exponential-norm-bound.title: Bounds for the Exponential
thm-exponential-norm-bound.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and write a=‖A‖. Then

  1. ‖eA‖≤ea;
  2. ‖eA−I‖≤ea−1;
  3. ‖eA−I−A‖≤ea−1−a≤a2ea2.

In particular ‖etA‖≤e|t|a for every real t.

thm-gelfand.title: Gelfand’s Formula
thm-gelfand.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and let ‖⋅‖ be any matrix norm on Mn(C). Then

limk→∞ ‖Ak‖1/k=ρ(A).

In particular the limit exists and does not depend on which matrix norm is used.

thm-neumann-series.title: Neumann Series with a Bound
thm-neumann-series.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) with ‖A‖<1, and write a=‖A‖. Then:

  1. I−A is invertible, and ∑k≥0Ak=(I−A)−1;
  2. ‖(I−A)−1‖≤11−a;
  3. for every K≥0, the partial sum SK=∑k=0KAk satisfies ‖(I−A)−1−SK‖≤aK+11−a;
  4. ‖(I−A)−1‖≥11+a.

thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius.title: Norms Close to the Spectral Radius
thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius.title_html: Norms Close to the Spectral Radius
thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and let ε>0. Then there is a norm ‖⋅‖t on Cn whose induced operator norm satisfies

ρ(A)≤‖A‖t≤ρ(A)+ε.

thm-norm-equivalence.title: Equivalence of Norms in Finite Dimension
thm-norm-equivalence.title_html: Equivalence of Norms in Finite Dimension
thm-norm-equivalence.html: Let V be a vector space over F=R or C with dim⁡V=n<∞. Then any two norms on V are equivalent. Explicitly, if B=(v1,…,vn) is a basis of V, if ‖⋅‖2 denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector, ‖∑ixivi‖2:=(|x1|2+⋯+|xn|2)1/2, and if N is any norm on V, then there are constants 0<m≤M with m‖v‖2 ≤ N(v) ≤ M‖v‖2for every v∈V.

thm-normal-equations-squares-conditionin.title: The Normal Equations Square the Condition Number
thm-normal-equations-squares-conditionin.title_html: The Normal Equations Square the Condition Number
thm-normal-equations-squares-conditionin.html: Let m≥n≥1 and let A∈Mm×n(C) have rank n. Then A∗A∈Mn(C) is invertible, and κ2(A∗A)=κ2(A)2.

thm-operator-norm-formulas.title: Computing the 1-, 2- and Infinity-Norms
thm-operator-norm-formulas.html:
Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F) with m,n≥1. Then

  1. ‖A‖1=max1≤j≤n ∑i=1m|aij|, the largest absolute column sum;
  2. ‖A‖∞=max1≤i≤m ∑j=1n|aij|, the largest absolute row sum;
  3. ‖A‖2=σ1(A), the largest singular value of A (@def-singular-values).

thm-operator-norm-properties.title: Properties of the Operator Norm
thm-operator-norm-properties.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on each of Fn, Fm, Fℓ, and let A∈Mm×n(F). Then:

  1. ‖Ax‖≤‖A‖‖x‖ for every x∈Fn, and ‖A‖ is the smallest constant with this property;
  2. ‖⋅‖ is a norm on the vector space Mm×n(F);
  3. ‖In‖=1;
  4. ‖AB‖≤‖A‖‖B‖ for every B∈Mn×ℓ(F). In particular the operator norm induced on Mn(F) by a single norm on Fn is a matrix norm in the sense of @def-matrix-norm.

thm-parallelogram-characterization.title: The Parallelogram Law Characterizes Inner-Product Norms
thm-parallelogram-characterization.title_html: The Parallelogram Law Characterizes Inner-Product Norms
thm-parallelogram-characterization.html: Let F be R or C, let V be a vector space over F, and let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on V. Then there is an inner product on V with ⟨v,v⟩=‖v‖2 for every v if and only if ‖⋅‖ satisfies the parallelogram law (∗) for all u,v∈V. When it exists, that inner product is unique.

thm-perturbed-inverse-bound.title: Relative Error in a Perturbed Solve
thm-perturbed-inverse-bound.title_html: Relative Error in a Perturbed Solve
thm-perturbed-inverse-bound.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible, let b≠0, and let x be the solution of Ax=b. Let E∈Mn(C) and f∈Cn be perturbations with r=‖A−1‖‖E‖<1, and let x~ be the solution of (A+E)x~=b+f, which exists and is unique by @cor-invertible-matrices-open. Then ‖x~−x‖‖x‖≤‖A‖‖A−1‖1−r(‖E‖‖A‖+‖f‖‖b‖).

thm-relative-error-bound.title: Relative Error Under Perturbation of the Data
thm-relative-error-bound.title_html: Relative Error Under Perturbation of the Data
thm-relative-error-bound.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible, let b≠0, and let Ax=b.

  1. (Perturbing b.) If Ax~=b+Δb, then ‖x~−x‖‖x‖≤κ(A)‖Δb‖‖b‖, and there are b and Δb for which equality holds.
  2. (Perturbing A.) Let E∈Mn(C) with r:=κ(A)‖E‖/‖A‖<1. Then A+E is invertible; and if (A+E)x~=b, then ‖x~−x‖‖x~‖≤κ(A)‖E‖‖A‖,‖x~−x‖‖x‖≤r1−r.

thm-roots-depend-continuously.title: Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients
thm-roots-depend-continuously.title_html: Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients
thm-roots-depend-continuously.html: Let n≥1 and let p(x)=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c1x+c0∈C[x] be monic, with roots μ1,…,μn∈C listed with multiplicity (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits). Let ε>0. Then there is δ>0 with the following property. If q(x)=xn+bn−1xn−1+⋯+b1x+b0 is monic of the same degree n and |bj−cj|<δ for every j, then the roots ν1,…,νn of q, listed with multiplicity, can be numbered so that |νi−μi|<ε(i=1,…,n).

thm-spectral-radius-le-norm.title: The Spectral Radius Is a Lower Bound for Every Norm
thm-spectral-radius-le-norm.title_html: The Spectral Radius Is a Lower Bound for Every Norm
thm-spectral-radius-le-norm.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. If ‖⋅‖ is the operator norm on Mn(C) induced by a norm on Cn (@def-operator-norm), then ρ(A)≤‖A‖.
  2. More generally, ρ(A)≤‖A‖ for every matrix norm ‖⋅‖ on Mn(C) (@def-matrix-norm).
